profiles.name: Victor Williams
profiles.description: Victor Williams, also known as Vic Williams, was a British Army gunner who deserted rather than deploy to the Gulf War. He spoke publicly against the war before surrendering. In September 1991 a court-martial sentenced him to 14 months in civilian prison. This is a United Kingdom case.

profiles.name: Mutope Duguma
profiles.description: Mutope Duguma, identified by CDCR as James Daren Crawford, is a New Afrikan writer and participant in California’s prisoner hunger-strike movement. He has argued that officials used his political beliefs to justify prolonged isolation under a gang classification he disputed. In June 2012, the California Court of Appeal upheld his right to send a political letter to the San Francisco Bay View; that decision concerned censorship and did not release him from prison. CDCR listed him at California State Prison, Los Angeles County on September 10, 2026. The case recorded here concerns segregation within his earlier criminal sentence.

profiles.name: Ali Khalid Abdullah
profiles.description: Ali Khalid Abdullah was a Black Muslim anarchist and Michigan prison organizer. He was imprisoned in 1990 after an attempted action against businesses he said were fronts for a drug dealer accused of abusing a child. Abdullah and supporters said the group left without taking money or harming employees; he was convicted of assault with intent to rob while armed and sentenced to six and a half to twenty years. Inside prison he organized against racism and prison conditions, helped build the Political Prisoners of War Coalition, wrote extensively, and was repeatedly denied parole. Contemporary support material said his maximum discharge date was in July 2008. Later movement histories report that he was released and subsequently died, but the exact dates have not been established.
profiles.finding: Freedom Archives APLAN and Black Flag writings match Michigan organizer. Iraqi brigadier photograph rejected as unrelated.

profiles.name: Charles King
profiles.description: Charles King is a lawyer, minister and co-founder of Housing Works who became a leading advocate for homeless people living with HIV and AIDS. During New York demonstrations in the late 1990s and 2000, police repeatedly held King and other Housing Works activists overnight for minor protest offenses rather than issue appearance tickets. A 2001 civil settlement ended that city policy. The available court summary does not enumerate King’s individual arrest dates, so the separate overnight stays cannot yet be totaled exactly.

profiles.name: Nasser Ahmed
profiles.description:
Nasser Ahmed became a prominent figure in late-1990s civil-liberties disputes over the use of “secret evidence” in immigration detention. An Egyptian immigrant living in Brooklyn, he became linked—through community and legal work—to the orbit of the high-profile prosecution of Omar Abdel-Rahman, and U.S. immigration authorities treated him as a national security concern.

He was detained in 1996 and spent years in solitary confinement while the government relied on classified allegations that he and his lawyers could not fully review or rebut. The case drew sustained organizing and legal challenges, and immigration adjudicators later concluded that, once a declassified version of the allegations was available for meaningful rebuttal, key claims did not hold up. He was ultimately released, and his detention became a central example cited by critics of secret-evidence procedures.
profiles.finding: ACLU and congressional report match secret-evidence case; CMS detention report contains images needing caption verification. Nasser al-Bahri and astronomer rejected.
profiles.rights: No image selected; original credit and rights verification pending.

profiles.name: Roberto Jose Maldonado
profiles.description:
Roberto Jose Maldonado was one of the defendants prosecuted in connection with the Los Macheteros–linked case arising from the 1983 Wells Fargo depot robbery. His case centered on conspiracy allegations rather than claims that he personally carried out the vault theft, reflecting prosecutors’ broader effort to criminalize the organization’s support structure and financial networks.

He was convicted on a conspiracy count and sentenced to five years in federal prison, along with a monetary fine. The outcome positioned him among those punished for alleged coordination and facilitation within a politically motivated underground campaign.

Federal Bureau of Prisons records show that he left federal custody on March 3, 1993; his exact commitment date remains unresolved.
